utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday, the 14th of January, 2010. I would like first of all to greet the accused, Defence counsel, all the honourable members on the team of the OTP, and all the people assisting us in the courtroom. And I should also greet the witness once he enters the courtroom. I believe Mr. Kovacic wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours, good morning everybody in the courtroom. [Interpretation] I thought practical reasons it would be a good idea to resolve immediately the issue of protection of the next witness because technical preparations are needed, and we shouldn't do that at the 11th hour. That witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, we'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wanted to avoid mentioning names, but this is safe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. West, you have 42 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, please take a seat. One moment, Mrs. West, I have a question arising out of my thoughts during the night. Please have a seat, sir. Colonel, I have a small follow-up question for you. Yesterday, as you saw, we looked at a document relating to this famous meeting which took place in the month of November. You were seizing the political authorities during this meeting of a number of issues, and I had called your attention to item 6 that related to the line of command which you wanted to be unique. Since then I have thought about it some more, and I must tell you this: There is a discussion on the fact whether there was or not a single line of command at the time. General Praljak himself explained to us that after the events on the 9th of May of which he knew nothing at all, he had a discussion with Mr. Tuta. I shall not go into the details of this discussion. Other elements lead us to believe that there might have been a line of command with Boban, Naletilic, a direct line of command between the two, without the minister of defence being advised of it at all or the Chief of Staff for that matter and even the commander of the operational zones or the brigade commanders. Since you were an officer on the ground, you met your colleagues from time to time, you held meetings with your superiors. Did you have any knowledge of the existence of any other chain of command, non-traditional chain of command, since as definitions go the real chain of commands goes from the head of state right down to the lower levels in a traditional manner. It seems that the line of command went from the chief of -- head of state to a specialised unit and then other factions. What did you hear at the time about the existence of a dual chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my position as chief of artillery in the military district did not give me great opportunity to acquire information of that sort, but to the extent that I know, and I had some information which I believe was correct, and that is that there was a direct line of command between Mr. Boban and that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling us something important. You learned that there was a chain of command that established this line between Boban and the head of the units. Does this mean that in military terms that the minister of defence was sidelined, the Chief of Staff, and the commander of the operational zone were sidelined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I would like to insist a bit on this. You have been very cautious in your answer. First you've said this is not something that you had much opportunity. I quote your position: "... did not give me great opportunity to acquire information of that sort ..." And then you add that, I quote again: "To the extent that I know, and I had some information which I believe was correct, and that is that there was a direct line of command ..." Now, could you tell us where you had received such information and what it consists? Could you explain us on what this putative knowledge, I think it can be called, of yours is based? Did Mr. Praljak tell you? Did Mr. Naletilic tell you? Did Mr. Boban tell you? Was this a subject of conversation among your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a number of members of this unit share the same birthplace with me, and of course I had occasion to run into them from time to time. And from contacts with them I concluded that they were receiving orders directly from the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Which unit would that be you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the unit that was named a moment ago as Tuta's unit, but originally it was called the Convicts' Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And were there -- among these people were there any higher officers of that unit, or were -- was it simple soldiers that told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we take the middle level of that unit, officers not of the highest rank but still officers whom I trusted at the time. I trusted their information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours; good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maric. Sir, I just want to take up where Judge Trechsel left off, and I just want to clarify a little bit of what you just said. Should we understand then that you've never seen a document evidencing this direct line of command between Boban and the Convicts' Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not see a document that would confirm that, but I said a moment ago that I had information from people who were quite important in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's talk about those people. Are those just two people or more than two people?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically it's one of the commanders who unfortunately lost his life while liberating Rastani on the 24th of August, 1993. He was a commander in that unit, and he's from the same neighbourhood as I.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you've had -- this information is based on a conversation with only one person; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. If you give me time I can remember some more names of people who told me the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Go ahead, what are the other names?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One platoon commander who also lost his life in a hunting accident, Mr. Stojcic, a platoon commander in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's two people. Is there a third?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could recall, although it was a long time ago, for example, Mr. Sopta, but not the general. There were more than one person called Sopta in that unit. And some more soldiers of lower ranks in the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a confirmation of what I'm saying could be that I as a chief never had the opportunity to plan any use of artillery in direct support to that unit, and it's hard to imagine that in three years of war I would not have to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, the individual you called Mr. Sopta, what's his first name?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His father's name is Vinko. We called him Dok.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And where -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in our part of the world, nicknames are used a lot more than real names, like additional names for certain neighbourhoods --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, a particular neighbourhood can be called three different names.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Where does Mr. Sopta live today?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This gentleman, Mr. Sopta is no longer alive. A vast majority from that unit and from the HVO are dying to this day. Just before I left in order to come here, one of my fellow combatants was on his death-bed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, then you've mentioned three individuals who gave you this information, but all three individuals, as I understand it, are dead. But then you said some more soldiers of lower ranks in the same unit, is that right, gave you the same information as well?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could probably remember if I gave it some more thought. I could remember some names of persons at lower ranks. However, the fact remains that this unit was very rarely in contact and in the zone of my interest. So I did not have the duty to take care of the members of that unit --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so it is hard to remember -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, can you give us any one name of a soldier in that unit who's still alive today that gave you this information?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Robert, I can't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So again, I'll repeat my question. Can you give me a first and last name, a first and surname, of any person alive today who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Names, yes; surnames, not really.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So you cannot fully identify anyone who is alive today who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tried to remember after 17 years -- even if I try to remember the names of the people who were closest to me, even with the best of intentions, I need a lot of time to remember their names unless I have certain documents from that time before me --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one matter. Secondly, please take into account the fact that my health is seriously impaired, and you must trust me that I have indeed forgotten certain facts regarding names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric, we'll move on. Yesterday when we -- towards the end we were talking about -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We will move on to something else, but you gave us a technical detail that was quite interesting. You said that throughout your period of command you were never associated to a support to the unit commanded by Naletilic, and that was a bit surprising for you. Does this mean that Naletilic's unit, as far as weapons are concerned, had its own artillery, mortars, and so on, and maybe they were well equipped? And because of that, notably if they were acting outside the chain of command, didn't need to have logistical support and artillery support provided by an artillery unit that would be in the line of command under the chain -- the staff or that would be also an artillery unit that depended from the operational zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All manoeuvre units that were established in the HVO were not of extremely large capacity. But in relation to infantry units and brigades, they were, within the military districts, better equipped, and they had their own resources for support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. West, you may move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, yesterday we were talking about the Old Bridge and some orders in regard to it. And specifically we were talking about a November 8th packet order from Petkovic, and in turn a November 8th order from Lasic to shell the town of Mostar selectively on that day. And that was the day before the bridge finally came down. I noted in my questions to you that there was no specific targeting language in the November 8 orders, and you gave an explanation. And you're going to see that on your screen, on the Sanction screen in front of you. This is from transcript 48349, if you look right in front of you. I was looking at the orders and I said that the order said: "'Shell the city of Mostar selectively at different time intervals.'" And I said: "Is that language familiar to you?" And I believe we were looking at the Lasic order. You said: "Yes." And I said: "Because it appears that Lasic just took the Petkovic order and forwarded it down the chain of command; correct?" Your answer was: "Yes." And then I asked: "... whether this order specifically articulated targeting the bridge or not, and isn't that exactly what happened on November 8th?" You said: "I don't see a reference to the bridge as a target." And I said: "No, that's exactly right. You don't see specific language of the bridge as a target, but isn't it a fact, yes or no, that on November 8th the Old Bridge was targeted by the HVO?" And your answer was this: "Under item 2 it says selectively shelling." You said: "At that moment the HVO knew about military targets and their nature, and that referred exclusively to those military targets which were under the war doctrine served for the purpose of military units. They were used for the planning and conduct of combat activities and operations." So, Mr. Maric, my question today for you is: Yesterday when you said this, were you suggesting that these orders that say "selective targeting," the reason they said that was because those military targets were already so well known by the HVO that there was no reason to list them? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Don't you agree that such ambiguity in language, such unclear language, could potentially lead to confusion as to what the target was, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour, to the term "unclear language."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't accept the objection. "Ambiguity" means unclear. I think the witness can determine what I mean by that. I'll ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, don't you agree that such ambiguity in language, such unclear language, could potentially lead to confusion as to what the target was, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There can be no confusion --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that is a period when -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this would -- language in an order like this would have been out of the ordinary, would it not? It would have been unusual?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the logic of military thinking is probably rather different from the logic of legal thinking. The logic of military thinking --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, that's not my question. Excuse me, that was not my question. Let me say it again, and you can answer. Let's try it again. So my question was --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead, do repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- would this language in the order, would this have been out of the ordinary, would it not, it would have been unusual? The answer to that question is: Yes, no, or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not really fair. The answer to a question of that nature can perfectly reasonably require some explanation. The witness is being asked by a lawyer about a military document, and his answer, the introduction he was giving, is his answer as a military person giving evidence, and it's entirely reasonable that he should preface and give his explanation and answer to Ms. West's question in this way. And the interruption of his answer a few minutes ago was inappropriate. He should have been allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. West, you are a lawyer, you know the law. I'm sure that the colonel has some inkling of the law, but he's not a legal expert himself. So if your question has legal aspects, and he says, No, I'm not -- don't think so, you can ask him some additional information. If he answers, No, and then you go on to move on to something else, any reasonable trier of fact will think that he is right because you're not going into details, you're not pressing on, which is why Mr. Stewart actually rose to his feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a another question instead, Mr. Maric, and we're going to go to some more of the testimony from yesterday. I asked you a question in regard to that very same language I was asking you about, selective targeting and whether targets should be listed in orders. And I said --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can just have a moment, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So yesterday I was talking about the same order, and I said: "It said: 'Shell the town of Mostar selectively at various intervals.' "Mr. Maric, in your experience in military -- well, in your experience, when orders were issued regarding offensive operations, did they normally include a specific targeting information? We've seen a couple." And your answer from yesterday was: "Yes." Sir, do you remember that testimony from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, distinguished Prosecutor, I cannot remember everything I said exactly, but I shall confirm that when planning assault activity, it is necessary, inter alia, to point out specifically if one is planning attacks with a view to taking territory of the other side. Then the directions and objectives are spelled out in very specific terms. In the documents from this time that are being discussed yesterday and today, there were no concrete orders on attacks; namely, to abandon one's own positions and to penetrate enemy territory. The term used here is activity against enemy objectives.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is stated -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yesterday I also showed you a document which was from the night of November 8th, and it was a report from Lasic who had written that at 8.10 that morning the HVO tank had been firing from Stotina that whole day, and it fired 50 projectiles on the Old Town. Now I want to show you another document, and it should be directly in front of you. It's P09992; I opened up your binder to that page. P09992. This is a report from November 9th, so the day the bridge came down, and it's a report from 1900 hours that evening, and it's from Lasic. Number 1 is combat activity of the enemy, and then number 2 is entitled "our forces." And it says: "Defenders firmly hold their positions. And on provocation coming from the Muslim army, they returned fire from time to time. They did not return fire at the Chetniks." But then the next paragraph says: "In addition to the fire from infantry weapons at around 10.00 -- 1000 hours our tank fired few projectiles at a target which was determined earlier. At around 1015 hours our reconnaissance people from Hum reported that the Old Bridge was torn down, and they could not say anything about the cause of its destruction." Sir, I want to focus on the language here that says "a target which was determined earlier." This is unusual language in a report like this, is it not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, distinguished Prosecutor, I shall go back a day or two or several hours --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to a response I gave to one of the Prosecutor's questions where I was --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Apologies for the interruption. Mr. Maric, excuse me, stop.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My question was quite clear, and the answer in this case certainly is a yes or no. Let's try it again. I want to focus on the language here which says "a target that was determined earlier." This is unusual language in a report like this, is it not? Sir, can you answer that question yes or no or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 9th of November at 4.00, I went to reconnoitre --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, this has nothing to do with --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the southern part of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, I have refrained from asking for an order for you to be responsive. I have refrained from doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I understand that you want to give us additional information to explain. I understand why you're doing this, but this is a specific procedure. Here the Prosecutor is entitled to put questions, but she needs an answer yes or no. A yes or no answer, and if you don't agree, just say no. And if Ms. West wants to know why you are saying no, then she can press on and put another question to you. As I told you earlier, if she's not pressing on, I will infer from this that you're telling the truth. So it's up to her to conduct the game. She puts questions to you, answer by yes or no, and if she wants to contradict you because she doesn't agree with your answer, negative answer, then she has to provide you with additional information, and then you can develop what you want to say. I know that you want to explain yourself. In my own procedure in my own country, there would be no problem with that, and we would spend hours on all of this. And the trial would have been over ages ago. But this is another type of procedure, it's very lengthy, even though we're supposed to have a quick trial according to the Security Council. So, please, we have to follow the procedure. So answer by yes or no, and if Mrs. West wants to press on, she will. Anyway, I will have a question later on. So please answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, isn't it true that the target determined that's referenced here was the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you agree that the target determined earlier could have been the subject of discussions between Lasic, the author of this report, and Praljak at the meeting that took place 48 hours earlier on November 7th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, witness, I have a question regarding your previous answers. You were asked whether the target that was determined was the Old Bridge. Now we're talking about an order given to tanks, and you have told us that tanks are not part of the artillery. How do you know what kind of order was given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what kind of order was issued to them, but if the order was given from a higher level to the level where I operated, then I would have to have that order before me at some point in time, either immediately or later. Because professional organs had the possibility of seeing all orders that came from higher instances and also all orders that were elaborated at military district level and that went further down the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't find that a very clear answer. Isn't it a fact that you do not really know what was the previous target that is mentioned in this report? Have you seen the order? You have explained that it should come down and you should have the possibility to see it. That's not enough. That's not enough. You have clearly said no, you don't know -- no, it was not that target, and I want to know on what this was based.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I base my answer on the fact that I did not see such an order and that I did not hear of such an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't then the correct answer be: I don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know, if that's the best -- I don't know, I'm not a lawyer; I'm a soldier. I don't know. I don't know what's best for lawyers. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's not a matter that you have to be a lawyer to understand. Either you don't know, then you can say it was not this; or, as it turns out now, you cannot positively know, and then you should not give the answer that you think would be the desirable answer, the -- what would have been the right thing. But you have to say "I don't know." Otherwise it's not the truth, what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, if you just look at the question that was put by my colleague, Ms. West, her question was: Isn't it true that, et cetera ... so the witness was responding to the question as it had been put, and he answered from his point of view, namely, that it is not true. Had the -- had my colleague put the question in a more open-ended way, perhaps his answer would have been: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, in the document that is on the screen, there is a culpatory element. It says, and I quote: "In addition to the fire from infantry weapons, at around 1000 hours our tank fired few projectiles at a target which was determined earlier." You're black on white -- black and white it is written that the Old Bridge which must be the target, because in the following sentence there is mention of the Old Bridge, was determined as a target or had been determined as a target. Maybe the officer in charge of drafting this report did a poor job. But still when you read all this, as Mrs. West is submitting, it seems that there was a plan to fire at the old bridge, and here we have a report saying that this has been done. There were shots, projectiles were fired, and the Old Bridge fell down, was torn down. Then the person drafting the report says, We know nothing about the cause of the destruction. Now, militarily-wise, I'm not looking at -- thinking about liability or responsibility here. I'm just thinking about what happened in terms of military -- in terms of military. Can a tank fire at a bridge if this objective has not been predetermined?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was actually -- we try not to do a double act, but my point is a separate one from the one that Ms. Alaburic made, which of course I support. But when Judge Trechsel put at page 20, line 19, to the witness: Well, wouldn't then the correct answer be: I don't know? Which is a perfectly normal way of cross-examining, and I don't mean that offensively, that is the sort of question which might be put in cross-examination of a witness. But with respect it's not really fair in the light of what the witness has said, because what the witness is saying - and that's a clear -- I'm not arguing the case. I'm simply pointing out what's on the transcript. He's saying that he bases his answer on the fact that he did not see such an order, and I did not hear of such an order, but that has to be linked with what he has clearly said a few lines above, which is if there had been such an order, he would have seen it. And on that basis the answer: No, there was no -- no such order, that wasn't the position, is perfectly fair. Now, Your Honours may or may not accept in the end, that's for Your Honours' judgement, the ingredients that go into the witness's answer. Your judgements as to whether he is or isn't telling the truth on particular points is ultimately Your Honours' judgement. But the way that Judge Trechsel, with respect, then put the -- and it is a cross-examination point to the witness, really did not take proper account of what the witness had given fairly and squarely as his answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point, Your Honours. I would now like to say something about the translation. I must say that I'm not sure whether the translation is good or not, so I would like to ask our colleagues from the interpretation booths to look at the formulation. In the Croatian text we have a neutral formation, as it were, where a verb is used, and it is stated around 1015, Our reconnaissance from Hum informed us that the bridge was destroyed. The formulation was not that someone destroyed the bridge or that the bridge just collapsed on its own. It is indefinite. But the -- the translation is "was torn down." I'm a lay person as far as the English language is concerned, but it seems to me that the English version suggests that someone tore down the bridge, whereas the Croatian version keeps this neutral formulation, that the bridge was destroyed, but that we don't know -- we don't know who destroyed it or how. If I could ask Sinisa and the lady to help us out with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me return to my question because the interventions from the two lawyers threw us a little bit astray. So in your language it seems that the tank is firing at a target which was determined earlier. Militarily-wise, when a tank is firing a projectile, is it firing at predetermined targets or is -- can the tank crew just fire anywhere? Are they free to fire anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, fire is opened at targets that had been set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to move to P06564. Sir, it's in your binder. It's marked on top 0564 [sic], and we're going to go to page 2 of the English, and it's -- the page of the B/C/S, it's the only page. P06564.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a report from November 10th, 1993, signed by Lasic. And it begins: "On November 9th between 1015 and 1020 the Stari Most, Old Bridge, fell into the Neretva River. And I'm hereby sending you the information that we have in connection." And there's number 1 which talks about the damage, number 2 talks about the Serbs. Number 3 says the Old Bridge was in the vicinity of the line of separation. Number 4 talks about the bridge not being marked. But then we come to number 5, and it talks about targeting. And let's read that. It says: "HVO units never targeted the Old Bridge, and destroying it was not the aim. Defending themselves against numerous attacks by the MOS from the direction of the Old Bridge towards Podhum and the Franciscan church where there were many breakthroughs of the defence line, units fired at the enemy's manpower and materiel near the bridge. The Old Bridge was destroyed as a consequence of combat operations because that area has been the scene of fierce clashes since the beginning of the conflict." Mr. Maric, doesn't it appear here, doesn't it appear to you, that Lasic is denying that the bridge was targeted, but at the same time gives an excuse as to why the HVO brought it down? Claimed it was an accident, claimed it wasn't deliberate, claims that it was the result of units fired at the enemy's manpower and materiel near the bridge; isn't that a correct summary, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question by the distinguished Prosecutor implies that Lasic said that they had destroyed the Old Bridge, which I cannot see in this document. I also have to say I'm seeing this report for the first time because on the 9th, after I returned from command reconnaissance in the southern theatre, 50 kilometres away from Mostar, in view of my injuries and later health problems, I was bedridden for the next 12 days -- 20 days. And if I have to look at a document for the first time, I agree to analyse it from the military point of view, but I was not a witness to these events. I didn't even see the documents at the time because, as I said, I was in a bad way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, don't you agree with me that it appears from paragraph 5 that Lasic admits, concedes, indicates, that the HVO brought down the bridge but he just didn't put it on paper that the HVO had actually targeted it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm reading what it says here. I don't know what Commander Lasic was thinking or what he meant. I don't see it written that the HVO had destroyed the bridge. Madam Prosecutor, I heard from you in the last three or four hours of examination a number of terms that I could have reacted to, spending more than 30 minutes of your time. And trying to understand you, I tried to answer as best I could. But reading someone's thoughts 17, 20 years later is very hard --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just focus on the second sentence here. He's saying: "Defending themselves against numerous attacks," and there he's talking about his own units, "from the direction of the MOS ... there were many breakthroughs of the defence line." And then he says: "Units," HVO units, "fired at the enemy's manpower and materiel near the bridge." You would agree with me that what that refers to is units, HVO units, firing at materiel near the bridge; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in operations against the Army of Republika Srpska, especially when crossing the bridge, I lost one man who did not belong to my unit, but I know that one soldier was hit -- killed there --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I can't begin to imagine how the beginning of that sentence could be responsive to my --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One sentence, and then you will have your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please give it.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thus, at certain moments the Old Bridge could have been identified as a legitimate military target. And it's possible that fire was opened at it in order to neutralise certain parts of enemy manpower.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you agree with me that there's a real possibility that all these orders indeed do talk about targeting the Old Bridge, sir? Is that the conclusion you're giving the Court?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You just said it's a real -- you just said that it's possible that fire was opened at it in order to neutralise certain parts of enemy manpower. Fire was opened at it. It is possible, you just said, that fire is opened at it. When you said "it," you meant the Old Bridge ; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think we have to be careful because the question put is not the same. There's much more in the question that Ms. West just put to the witness than what he had already said. So to suggest that all her question is doing is reflecting what he's already said, which would raise another question as to why we're wasting our time going over the same ground again, is actually not fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sure this can be addressed on re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I'll continue. The next sentence is: "The Old Bridge was destroyed as a consequence of combat operations." Sir, when you look at all of paragraph 5, you read the whole thing, don't you agree that what Mr. Lasic is saying here is that the HVO brought down the bridge, whether it was targeted or not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree that one can conclude from this sentence that the HVO destroyed the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to move to another subject unless the Chamber has any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, according to this document which I'm looking at, Mr. Lasic provides an explanation, the following explanation. He says that the Muslim units, let's say the ABiH, were by the bridge and that was -- and that there was equipment there. And then he said that there were clashes since the beginning of the conflict, and this was a clash seen. He then adds that the ABiH, because the bridge was seemingly located in the geographical area of the ABiH, they did not hoist the flag of UNICEF, because had they hoisted the UNICEF flag, things might have been different in that case. He then says that the HVO never targeted the Old Bridge and destroyed it. And then he added that they needed to defend themselves against numerous attacks of the Muslims coming from the Old Bridge. This is what he says. I, and as I'm sure you did also, we watched the videos. There were videos of this. When I see that tank firing, we can also see tracer bullets. I believe the tracer bullets don't come from the tank. There are tracer bullets and there are projectiles which hit the Old Bridge. But during this scene I didn't hear shots coming from the ABiH. I don't have the feeling that there was any exchange of fire then. I believe it is the tank that is firing. There is no fighting ongoing which Mr. Lasic describes. Perhaps this was actually happening and perhaps the video was not very comprehensive. Let me get to my question now. When one needs to use the artillery, whether it be small pieces of artillery or heavy artillery, does one need to open fire because someone fires at you? Or can one fire because it has been planned militarily, when targets have been set, prior to firing; and in that case one states: At 1500 hours, at 1530, we shoot, we fire, and that all this has been planned beforehand because the ammunition needs to be loaded, the cannons need to cool down. And for a number of reasons the shots are spaced out. So my question is a very simple one: Is a cannon, artilleryman, or a tank -- member of a tank group just shoot? Or is he entitled to shoot outside the shooting targets or times if necessary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before your answer, I would like to already say that on page 28, lines 4 and 5, there is a mistake in -- on the screen that -- I believe that Judge Antonetti spoke not about the UNICEF, which is the United Nations Children's Fund, but he spoke about UNESCO, the flag of UNESCO, et cetera, et cetera, it is just for the correction of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my colleague had looked at the text, he would have seen that the text actually mentioned UNICEF and not UNESCO. It should have been the UNESCO flag, but we are dealing with legal matters here, and what we have in the document is UNICEF not UNESCO, but my fellow Judge did not see the document. So this is confusing, and when a question is summarised like this and I'm interrupted, I lose track. Well, anyway, would you like me to put the question again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer it if you could repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, right, so I shall repeat my question. Generally speaking my questions are very long because I'm very cautious. I must be very careful about what I say. In the document we have before us a flag is mentioned, a flag which the Muslims should have hoisted, a UNICEF flag, it should have been a UNESCO flag, but that is a point of detail. But Mr. Lasic then indicates that fighting has taken place and that the Muslims who were near the bridge were firing and that there were clashes. Therefore, Mr. Lasic concludes in paragraph 5 that the Old Bridge was never targeted as a target as such, and it was not destroyed with an aim and with a view to destroying the bridge, but fighting took place. So one can therefore conclude that the destruction of the Old Bridge is a consequence of the fighting. So if we go beyond that, I would like to put the question to you which runs as follows. So when a tank fires, when an artilleryman fires with a heavy weapon, does one fire at targets which are predetermined, preset targets? Or does one fire according to the events unfolding? And I would like to add that I told you on looking at the videos, one has a feeling that the tank crew fires at regular intervals, and on the video one cannot hear shots fired from the Muslims. Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly what you can see and hear in that footage. I didn't see it many times. I just don't like to watch it. But according to the rules, one opens fire at certain targets if your own life is threatened from that direction. Units or assets always have to be manned, regardless of whether it's an artillery weapon or an infantry weapon. So this fire targeting the area around the Old Bridge was certainly provoked by certain actions of the other side, and the bridge as a predetermined target did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we're going to go to P03899, P03899, and the pink tab -- sorry, the yellow tab's at the top, we'll give you that. This is a letter, August 2nd, 1993, signed by you. P03899. Do you recognise this, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a resignation letter, sir.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a letter whereby I, among other things, offered my resignation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. In the first paragraph, it's a bit of an introductory paragraph, but right in the middle you say: "I'm very worried about the way in which a large number of commanders, chiefs, assistants, clerks, and other important officials at all levels have been going about their assigned tasks and duties. I can no longer tolerate their total irresponsibility and indifference in the face of the alarming situation both in the operation zone and further afield." And in the next paragraph you wrote: "I cannot accept the fact that personal interests, cars, flats, and other personal concerns should be deemed more important than our principal and fundamental task of defending our homes and the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I can no longer accept to see by my side certain individuals, with whom I supposedly share the faith in our final success, whose moral and professional qualities are doing more harm than good to the common goal that we are fighting for." Now, I'm going to stop right there and ask you a little bit about your language. You had said, "our principal and fundamental task of defending our homes and the territory of the Croatian Community ..." Sir, when you wrote "homes," did that include the protections of Muslims and their homes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will avail myself of this opportunity to take just ten seconds to answer Madam Prosecutor, a question that I didn't answer a few days ago, namely, the names of some Muslim families in my neighbourhood. So as part of this answer let me say that in my neighbourhood, which is 90 per cent populated by Croats, there lived and there still live, and they participated in the defence as part of HVO units, several Muslim families, including family Palavdzic, which I mentioned before, and two other families, Hazirovic, by name. Those families are still in their homes, in their houses. At that time and still today they had the same views as I on the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, as regards this letter, Your Honours, when I came back home in the afternoon I was met by my wife, who is a colleague of yours, a lawyer, and she read -- she read a copy of this letter. And she said verbatim: Dear husband, from this moment on I have so much more love and appreciation for you because of what you have written, that I will never leave you until the day we die. But as a lawyer, I do find fault with certain formulations that can be ambiguous. I realise that I'm a soldier by training. I have no legal knowledge, and perhaps I put some things here that may sound ambiguous for somebody who's not a soldier, but at that time I was feeling like a man who was aware that the time was coming when he would have to leave his home and his town, and not alone but together with many other families because the military situation was so bad, our manpower levels were so low, we were under such threat on many defence lines, that it was perfectly clear that we might soon lose large swaths of territory in the environs in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric, and I think when I asked you when you wrote "homes" did that include the protection of Muslims and their homes as well, and I think your answer is yes. So I'd like to move on in this letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- no, no, I'm sorry, I thought you were going away from the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I'd like to go -- to continue on, and the next paragraph is: "I cannot understand certain individuals who are complacent about their own high ranks, for instance, the rank of colonel and are glad to be receiving a colonel's salary. They drive around in HVO cars. They have managed to get hold of flats and are enjoying all the privileges, and yet their contribution to our goal remains small or even non-existent." Mr. Maric, when you wrote "they have managed to get hold of flats and are enjoying all the privileges," can you please explain what you meant to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mostar was deep in my heart, and it still is. And whenever I had the time I toured positions of artillery units and the front lines alike. Only few people would do that, those who were born there and who knew their lay of the land and the disposition of features. And when I would find a soldier who had been in the trenches for several days with food supplies running late, with equipment supplies running late, they would complain because they had information that in certain departments there were available vehicles in sufficient numbers that were perfectly able to bring supplies to the front line. And the soldiers were very unhappy because bread, ammunition, or clothing was not delivered in time. And some people, especially from the logistics which are not known as great fighters, were trying to teach me lessons about how best to use these assets --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I'm going to stop you there.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And after the departure of a large number of Serb civilians --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was in regard to this sentence which was: "They have managed to get hold of flats are enjoying all the privileges ..." Sir, does that mean that HVO persons were taking flats that did not belong to them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to continue, Your Honours. After the departure of large numbers of --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I'm sorry again --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- officers of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can't continue. You can just answer the question: Yes, no, or I don't know. It was a very simple question. Does that mean HVO persons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, we have less than -- Madam Prosecutor has less than six minutes left, so her time is very precious. She is putting a question to you which you could expand on, but you could also say: No. And she will ask you: Why? She's asking you whether they occupied flats who belonged to Muslims. Then you say: Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wish to say that the question of my learned friend contains a legal formulation, namely, did they take apartments that did not belong to them, and that's the passage that cause -- causes ambiguity and requires explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I address you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You are in the hands of Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please listen to Mrs. West's questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, is your complaint here that people, soldiers, high-ranking soldiers, low-ranking soldiers, were taking over flats in West Mostar that were flats that were originally owned by Muslims who had been evicted? Is that your complaint?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not my complaint, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I would like to go to P02 --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask a follow-up question regarding this letter. Did that letter -- first, did you actually send it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I'm -- I'm glad if I can in response to your question clarify what I wrote in that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't need clarification of what you write because I think that the letter is pretty clear. The question is: Were there any consequences of this letter? Did any reaction -- you asked for a reaction. Was -- did any reaction come forward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were certain positive reactions, and I was satisfied that I had written the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Maric, we're going to go to P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question. Those who had an opportunity in their life to send a resignment letter, you know, it always takes courage to do so. And when you write such a letter you believe that people should understand that you are brave when you do this. When sending this kind of letter, didn't you risk anything, to be demoted or maybe expelled from the army? People would say: This is none of his business. What's his problem? It's -- we should just drive in our nice cars and have our nice flats, and he can be -- go on the front and get killed, and we're in the rear end, and can enjoy our privileges. This is a very human -- this is a reaction that can occur. You know, people understand that this kind of reaction can exist. Did you do this because you were totally disparate? You noted that there were no ammunition, that the political and military plans were not defined correctly, that your own soldiers were living in difficult conditions, when others would be parading in Mostar and elsewhere, in nice limousines, usually German limousines, is that why you were pushed into resigning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at that time I was quite aware of my position and of possible adverse consequences that could ensue. However, the people to whom I had addressed this letter knew perfectly well who I was and what kind of man I was. And I was not afraid of any adverse reactions from them. As for possible grumbling and negative reactions of some colleagues whom -- who were the subject of my letter, no, I was not afraid of them. That's why I wrote the letter in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think it's time for the break. You have less than five minutes left, Mrs. West. Maybe it would be best if you finished, and then we will break. So please finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P02879. This is a document that is dated June 21st, and this is signed by Mr. Coric. It's a request to issue decisions permitting occupancy of apartments. "We enclose a list of civilian apartments occupied by members of the military police and request that the corresponding decisions be issued as urgently as possible." Sir, this is several pages long, there are several names, it's 137 apartments. Mr. Maric, would you agree with me that at the time, in the summer of 1993, there was a practice, whereby the HVO evicted Muslim homeowners in West Mostar from their apartment and put their own HVO people in those apartments?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very --

utterances.speaker: MR. PLAVEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. This question and this document pertain to topics that were not part of the examination-in-chief. Civilian apartments are referred to here, not Muslim apartments, as the Prosecutor had put it in her question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. West, in this text there's no mention of Muslim flats, civilian flats here -- what it says is civilian flats occupied by members of the military police. Now, there was something he said earlier, and you didn't listen. He said that Serb officers also had left their apartments. I had inferred from this that HVO officers took occupancy of these flats. You have three minutes left, so if you could put your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I put the question in the words that I thought to be appropriate. And this gentleman can answer the question in any which way he wants. And the question was: Would you agree with me that at the time, in the summer of 1993, there was a practice that the HVO evicted Muslim homeowners in West Mostar from their apartments and put their own HVO people in those apartments?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, what's your answer?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look specifically at 80, and if we can go to Sanction, please. You see number 80 in front of you. That street that's mentioned, is that your street?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 80 is the former name of my current street.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right, okay. And number 25 of your street, before the war, do you know who lived in number 25?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My number is 202. That is pretty far away from number 25. I don't know who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now break for 20 minutes, after which we will have the re-direct, and then the testimony of this witness will be over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. As far as re-direct is concerned, I believe that we have Mrs. Alaburic. Mr. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since many topics were raised during the cross-examination by Ms. West that were not dealt with during the examination-in-chief, I will have a certain set of questions for our witness, Mr. Maric. Depending on your own interventions, Your Honours, it is my assessment that I should be done in about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put a question to you in relation to the last questions put to you by Ms. West. My learned friend Ms. West showed you your letter dated the 2nd of August, 1993, which is document P3899. She focused on the subject of apartments. After that she showed you P2879, which is a letter of the military police administration dated the 21st of June, 1993. In relation to that, I would like to put a question to you. Did you perhaps notice who the military police administration was addressing in this document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were addressing the office for housing and infrastructure to the attention of Mr. Mario Salavarda.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will get to that. But before that, please tell us, what was roughly the percentage of the Serb population of Mostar before the war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but between 20 and 30 per cent. I don't even know what the exact percentage of Croats was, never meant much to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From a Zagreb point of view, it was one-third Croat, one-third Muslim, and one-third Serbs, so let that be our working version. One-third were Serbs. Tell us in the territory of the municipality of Mostar, were there any significant units, facilities, institutions of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Mostar there were some very important facilities and institutions of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you were to describe whether there were relatively few or many officers who lived in Mostar and persons who lived in the -- worked in the Yugoslav People's Army, what would you say, few or many?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many. Mostar was a Mecca for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, at the moment when the operations for liberating Mostar were over, liberating them from the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of the Bosnian Serbs, how many Serb inhabitants remained in Mostar after that? Or, rather, tell us, did most of them leave or stay behind? That would do.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, these JNA officers and other JNA personnel, did they stay in Mostar, or did they leave with the army that had been expelled?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically all of them had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you were to answer the question of how many apartments stayed in Mostar that had previously been inhabited by Serbs, what would you say, many or a little?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many apartments that Serbs and members of the JNA lived in, socially-owned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you were to define the ownership of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You added that it was socially owned. We have -- we know this concept. I'm sure you know what it means. An apartment that is socially owned can only be allocated by an administrative entity, be it a civilian or a military entity. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Maric, were any regulations passed on the way in which these apartments would be allocated, the apartments that were previously in the hands of the Serbs? Were they given to the military, to civilians, to inhabitants of Mostar generally speaking who did not have apartments? Let me be very specific, for temporary use?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, regulations had been passed for the temporary use of abandoned apartments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you about this office for housing and communal affairs. Was this one of the bodies that made decisions regarding the temporary use of these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, you can put the question, but I believe that my previous question solved the problem -- solved the problem. If you want to waste time, go ahead, but we've already mentioned this. The documents were admitted. Any legal expert, even low-level legal expert know exactly what happens. You want to use all of your time, but I think you're wasting it right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope that you did not want to say through that, that even the worst possible lawyer would be able to handle if he or she were in my position. I simply want to deal with the document that Ms. West had shown. I want to be specific because there are many bodies in Herceg-Bosna that were in charge of allocating apartments for temporary use at the -- commissions at the level of the defence department, of the operative zone, and documents that we have admitted into evidence in this regard have to do with that. As far as I can remember, this particular matter had not been dealt with previously, and that is why my question this time had to do with this particular office, namely, whether this particular office had any role in the temporary allocation of apartments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the best of your knowledge, Mr. Maric, the civilian or military authorities of Herceg-Bosna, to the best of your knowledge, at any level did they organise the expulsion of Muslims from their apartments so that Croats could move in?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about some Muslims in West Mostar having been indeed expelled from their apartments and having a Croat move into these apartments?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of this problem of the Muslims being moved out, regardless of their numbers in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the level of talk, not at official meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you now as a citizen of Mostar. Had you heard of any such thing and -- well, if you haven't heard about it, then I cannot ask you anything else about this. So we can just move on then. In relation to the Old Bridge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Unless I'm lost, I do not see that there is an answer registered to your last question: Had you heard of any such thing? And then you say: Well, if you haven't heard about it ... But in between, I think one would expect an answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is in line 6, Your Honour. Line 6 of page 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I was a bit confused because then you put another question of -- on line 7 which is very similar, I must say. Then the witness says: "That was at the level of talk, not at official meetings." And then you continue: "I'm asking you now as a citizen of Mostar ..." Either that was completely unnecessary, or there must be, again, an answer. Our dialogue perhaps now clarifies, but I hope you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, basically I withdrew that question because as I was following what the witness has said, I realised that, except for a few rumours, he didn't really know anything about this. So I kindly ask you to take this as my withdrawal of this question or my conclusion. We can clarify this, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, the question here now is whether you, as a citizen of Mostar, at the time had heard of such a situation that Muslim was expelled from his or her apartment in West Mostar and that a soldier forcibly moved into the said apartment?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now a few questions in relation to the Old Bridge, Mr. Maric. I am going to refrain from using the notion "Old Bridge" in my questions, so please understand it that way. What -- do you know what it means when a particular facility or landmark has the status of a cultural monument?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you know about the laws of war and the extent to which you as a soldier know the law of war, can a cultural monument become a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any facility that is used for planning and executing combat operations by a military formation becomes a military target.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, the Muslim side in the conflict in Mostar, did they ever suggest in any way to protect the Old Bridge and to have the zone around the Old Bridge excluded from any kind of combat activity and be marked as such?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the activities of General Praljak in 1992, I am not aware of any other activities in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in a single sentence what kind of activities these were on the part of General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were activities of engineering protection provided to the Old Bridge in order to protect it from Serb shells. I'm surprised that General Praljak did not mention yesterday that before that the bridge had been hit several times already and significantly damaged, that is to say before the HVO units could physically get to the Old Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it ever use the Old Bridge for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Old Bridge as a facility was used very often by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for military purposes in order to transport military equipment across it and to cross it in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did the Old Bridge link the east bank with a small part on the west bank that was under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't agree that it's a small part exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, apart from the Old Bridge was there any other bridge that linked East Mostar with that part of the territories on the western bank that was under the control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one period of time during the war, a makeshift bridge was made that was used in order to cross to the right bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, could military equipment such as weapons, ammunition, et cetera, be transported across that makeshift bridge?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina have its own positions near the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina ever operate from positions near the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'm going to put a few questions to you in terms of the relationship between Boban and the Convicts' Battalion. We've prepared a set of documents for Your Honours and for you, Witness. They are a separate file here consisting of four documents, since that was discussed --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me, my apologies. Do you have a set for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, we don't. We have never prepared documents for you for re-direct. We never prepared documents for re-direct for you, but I'm now asking my case manager to e-mail these documents to Ms. West. I apologise for the fact that this hadn't been done, but obviously we didn't have enough time to co-ordinate everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I mean, I don't have the documents and they weren't on the original list. So, I mean, I can wait to see them, but I don't know that this is -- I don't have the documents -- thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you my set.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, indeed, our case has been on for several months, and we never printed documents for the re-direct, but we did send to our colleagues the list of documents that we would use in re-direct. I am sorry. I do apologise. We would have done that had we realised that our colleague wanted to have the documents in paper form as well in hard copy. We can now rely on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, please look at the first document, the first document 2D925. This is a brief letter of Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, addressed to Mate Boban. The date is the 1st of February, 1994, and here in the last line Tuta says of himself, "your personal advisor." Tell us, Mr. Maric, do you interpret that as some kind of a direct link between Mr. Naletilic and Boban, or do you think that this qualification should be interpreted in some other way?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A special link. I have no other explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document, 4D618. Mr. Maric, this is a diagram that was prepared by General Petkovic as a witness in the Blaskic case. That was about ten years ago. Before my question, tell me, Mr. Maric, while preparing for your testimony did we ever discuss the Convicts' Battalion and Mladen Naletilic, Tuta?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at this diagram. In this diagram the Convicts' Battalion is directly under the supreme commander as opposed to other units that are on the left-hand side of the diagram that are directly linked to the Main Staff. In view of your own understanding of this diagram, does it correspond to what you told us in court today who the Convicts' Battalion was subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again I would like to draw your attention -- or rather, no, no, this is fine. This is fine. This document is all right. Very well. I just wish to say that in the English translation of this document there is no direct link between the supreme commander and the Main Staff, which is very important because in some questions -- with regard to some questions, the Main Staff was directly subordinated to the supreme commander. So please bear in mind this mistake. We took this document over from the Blaskic case, and that's why we didn't intervene. 4D1356 is the next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is an interview by Ivan Andabak to the weekly "Globus" dated 17 March 2009 -- no, no, sorry, 2000. Do you know who Ivan Andabak was, Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to one passage. In Croatian it's on the last page and that part alone has been translated. To the question: "To whom were you responsible in terms of command during the war in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina?" General Andabak answered: "Exclusively to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, to Gojko Susak and to Mate Boban." The next question is, I quote: "And not to the minister of defence of Herceg-Bosna, Bruno Stojic, or to the commanders of the staff, Generals Milivoj Petkovic and Slobodan Praljak?" And the answer of Ivan Andabak reads: "We were responsible only to Susak and Boban." Tell us, Mr. Maric, does this answer from the commander of the Convicts' Battalion conform with what you told us in the courtroom earlier today?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next document is P226 -- correction, P5226. This is a report by the assistant head of the defence department in charge of security Ivica Lucic to President Mate Boban, dated 20th September 1993. The report refers to the Convicts' Battalion. Can you explain, Mr. Maric, the reason why the assistant head of the defence department addresses directly President Boban concerning the Convicts' Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only conceivable reason is that the person who signed this document believed or knew that President Boban was the superior of that unit, of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge about the general opinion of people in Mostar, did people in Mostar knew who commanded Tuta and the Convicts' Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could say anything, I would say it was the president himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say that the president was directly superior to this unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The first time did you say: If anyone commanded the unit, then it was the president?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And when you say "president," you mean who?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you a few questions now regarding the documents shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Alaburic. Of course this question which you raised a few minutes ago is a very important one, and we have already listened to the witness about this issue while -- while Ms. West has asked questions about who commanded the unit of Tuta. Now I would also like to ask you, Mr. Maric, if your knowledge is based on some hearsay or if you have had seen any documents about it, because when you confirmed here upon the question asked by Ms. Alaburic, you said that: "I could say that the president was directly superior to this unit." So now what kind of document or a kind of a order or whatever you based your position on? It is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, those units that were under the direct command of the military district or assault units commanded by the Main Staff were units that I met with frequently, and there was mutual assistance between us. They were the subject of certain orders and certain combat documents created at the level of the military district, and that is one of the reasons why I knew that those units were under the Main Staff. And this particular unit was not mentioned in these documents, and there's also the fact that I knew some of the members of that unit, and I had regional links with some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
